title: China port delays hit 10 days as Suez return threatens 2027
metaDescription: Shanghai and Ningbo berthing waits reach 10 days after typhoons. Suez return could cut global container demand 8.7% in H1 2027. Cosco orders 18 ships.
bottomLine: Ships are waiting 10 days to berth at Shanghai and Ningbo after Typhoon Saudel and weeks of earlier storms pushed 3.92 million TEU into queues. That is 11% of the global container fleet sitting idle. If carriers keep moving back to Suez, global head-haul container demand will contract 8.7% year on year in the first half of 2027, even if underlying cargo volumes keep growing.

stories.headline: Shanghai and Ningbo berthing waits hit 10 days after typhoons
stories.tldr: Ships are waiting 10 days to berth at Shanghai and Ningbo, with 3.92 million TEU held in queues worldwide after Typhoon Saudel.
stories.whatHappened:
Ships are now waiting 10 days to berth at Shanghai and Ningbo after Typhoon Saudel hit last week. The two ports handle more container volume than any others in the world. Linerlytica estimates the global logjam is holding up 3.92 million TEU, which is 11% of the global container shipping fleet. North Asia accounts for 54% of global port congestion, with around 2.5 million TEU of vessels waiting to berth.

APL Logistics said Saudel added to unprecedented levels of global port congestion following earlier typhoons including Bavi, Noul, Dolphin and Narra in recent weeks. Shanghai and Ningbo resumed operations on Friday, but APL Logistics warned that vessel bunching and accumulated backlogs would create continued congestion and schedule reliability challenges.

Freight rates remain firm on the transpacific. Asia-Europe is the exception, with rates dropping for two straight months due to falling demand. Charter rates have stayed high as newbuilding deliveries fell to a three-year low of 64,640 TEU in August due to summer holidays and fewer containerships having been ordered in early 2023. Eighteen new charters were recorded last week, with many ships above 4,000 TEU fixed forward months earlier.
stories.whyItMatters:
Your transit time just got longer and less predictable. A 10-day berthing wait adds two weeks to your Shanghai to Los Angeles lead time once you factor in the knock-on schedule slippage. If you have stock on the water right now with a planned arrival before mid-September, assume it will be late.

Carriers are scrambling for charter tonnage to replace redelivered ships, which means they are paying more and passing it through. Spot rates on the transpacific have held firm despite Asia-Europe falling for two months. You are paying for that berthing delay whether you see it on the invoice or not. Charter rates feed into contract renewals in Q4, so this congestion is already baked into your 2027 pricing.

If you are booking space for Q4 peak season, carriers have less capacity to sell because 11% of the global fleet is sitting in queues. Vessel availability is tight. You either book early and pay the rate, or you book late and pay more. There is no spare capacity waiting in reserve.
stories.hotTake: The typhoon season is not over. Saudel is the sixth named storm to hit Chinese ports in recent weeks, and we are still in the window for more. Carriers cannot fix schedule reliability while the weather keeps resetting the queue. If you are planning a November shipment and you have not booked space, you are already behind.
actions: Pull forward any shipments planned for late September to account for the berthing delay and schedule slippage
Confirm your carrier's vessel schedule and berthing slot before you load the container, not after
Add two weeks to your transit time assumptions for any Shanghai or Ningbo shipments until the queue clears

stories.headline: Suez return would cut global container demand 8.7% in H1 2027
stories.tldr: If all Asia-Europe services return to Suez by year-end, global head-haul container demand will contract 8.7% year on year in H1 2027.
stories.whatHappened:
Sea-Intelligence modelled the demand impact of carriers returning to Suez Canal routing. Currently 19% of Asia-Europe capacity is transiting the canal, following moves by Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd and MSC. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have shifted two Gemini services between Asia and the Mediterranean back to Suez. Maersk also moved its Middle East to US east coast MECL and West Africa to Middle East WAF6 services to Suez routings. MSC announced the return of four services: Jade and Tiger on Asia-Med, Albatross on Asia-North Europe, and Himalaya on Indian subcontinent-Mediterranean. CMA CGM has returned selected sailings, along with smaller operators including Fesco and CU Lines.

Sea-Intelligence assumes underlying demand growth remains at the average of the past 12 months, which is 6.6% year on year. If the current 19% Suez shift is the only change, global head-haul TEU-mile demand growth would slow to 3.8% year on year in the first half of 2027. If 50% of services returned to Suez between August and December, demand would contract by 1.1%. If all head-haul services revert to Suez by the end of the year, global head-haul container demand would fall 8.7% year on year in the first half of 2027.

Sea-Intelligence argued that a full return is the most realistic scenario if Suez routing proves operationally safe. Carriers maintaining services around Africa would continue to pay higher costs for longer transit times. The analyst expects some Europe-Asia back-haul services to continue routing around Africa, both for cost reasons and to absorb capacity, but stressed that market strength would be determined by head-haul demand.
stories.whyItMatters:
The Red Sea crisis generated a substantial increase in global container demand when measured in head-haul TEU-miles, which helped underpin the strong carrier market through 2024 and into 2026. Restoring shorter Suez routings reverses that effect. You are looking at negative demand growth in 2027 even if the underlying cargo volumes remain strong, purely because of shortening distances.

Carriers will have excess capacity once they stop burning miles around Africa. That will push rates down, but the timing matters. If the Suez return happens gradually through Q4 2026, you will see softer rates in Q1 2027. If it happens fast, rates could drop in November or December. Either way, your 2027 contract negotiations will be shaped by this shift.

You also need to watch transit time. Suez routing cuts 10 days off the Asia-Europe round trip compared with routing around Africa. That frees up capacity and shortens lead times, but it also means you need less inventory in the pipeline. If you have been managing to a 45-day transit and it drops to 35, you have cash tied up in stock you do not need.
stories.hotTake: Carriers will return to Suez as fast as their insurance and their shareholders let them. The cost difference is too large to ignore. The question is whether the Houthi threat has genuinely receded or whether carriers are just tired of losing money. I would not bet my Q1 2027 forecast on a stable Suez, but I would plan for lower rates.
actions: Model your 2027 freight budget with a 15% rate reduction on Asia-Europe lanes starting in Q1
Review your pipeline inventory levels if you ship Europe and adjust for a 10-day shorter transit time
Lock in any remaining 2026 shipments now before carriers start discounting to fill space in Q1

stories.headline: Cosco orders 18 ships, pushing global orderbook to record 14.84m TEU
stories.tldr: Cosco commissioned 18 ships worth $2.99 billion, bringing its orderbook to 1.89 million TEU and the global orderbook to a record 14.84 million TEU.
stories.whatHappened:
Cosco Shipping commissioned a dozen 22,000 TEU LNG dual-fuelled ships from Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding and six 3,200 TEU ships from CSSC Huangpu Wenchong Shipbuilding. The large ships, to be delivered between 2028 and 2030, are priced around $224 million each. The smaller vessels, to be built between 2028 and 2029, will cost $50.5 million each.

In April, Cosco ordered a dozen 13,600 TEU LNG dual-fuelled ships for $2.22 billion, for joint operations with affiliate OOCL, for delivery between Q3 2028 and Q1 2030. That followed a January commission for a dozen 18,000 TEU LNG dual-fuelled ships for $2.4 billion with similar delivery dates. Linerlytica's figures show Cosco's orderbook now at 1.89 million TEU, the largest behind MSC's 3 million TEU pipeline, exceeding CMA CGM's orders for 1.69 million TEU.

Cosco's owned fleet is now 2.78 million TEU, which could rise to 4.47 million TEU once all newbuildings are delivered. That would propel it to third place in the liner capacity rankings, displacing Maersk. Maersk's owned fleet totals 3.03 million TEU, and its orderbook is modest at 867,466 TEU. Assuming Maersk does not embark on a similar spending spree, its fleet could stand at 3.9 million TEU once all its newbuildings are delivered. Linerlytica said Cosco's latest orders bring the global orderbook to a new record high of 14.84 million TEU, representing 43.1% of the current fleet.
stories.whyItMatters:
Cosco is building to compete with MSC and CMA CGM in the top three carrier rankings, and it is doing it with large ships and LNG fuel. That has two consequences for you. First, more capacity coming online between 2028 and 2030 means lower rates in those years, assuming demand does not absorb it. Second, Cosco is betting on LNG as the fuel of the future, which means it expects carbon-related surcharges to be material enough to justify the capital cost.

The global orderbook is now 43.1% of the current fleet. That is the highest on record. Deliveries are concentrated in 2028 to 2030, so you have two years of tight capacity followed by a flood of new tonnage. If you are negotiating multi-year contracts, lock in 2027 rates now and renegotiate in 2028 when the newbuilds arrive.

Cosco's move to third place means you have one more carrier with global scale to negotiate with. That is good for competition, but only if Cosco prices to fill ships rather than to follow MSC and Maersk. Watch how Cosco prices its Asia-Europe contracts in Q4 2026. If it undercuts to gain share, you benefit. If it follows the market, you do not.
stories.hotTake: Cosco is betting $2.99 billion that demand will absorb 1.89 million TEU of new capacity by 2030. That is either visionary or reckless, depending on whether global trade grows or contracts in the next four years. I would not bet against Chinese state-owned enterprises getting the capital allocation wrong, but I would bet on them keeping the ships full by cutting rates.
actions: Negotiate 2027 contracts now before the market absorbs the Suez return and the Shanghai queue clears
Plan for softer rates in 2028 to 2030 when Cosco's newbuilds hit the water
Include Cosco in your carrier tender if you are not already using them, because they will need to fill 1.89 million TEU

stories.headline: Asia-Europe air freighter capacity up 18% despite ecommerce slump
stories.tldr: Freighter capacity from Asia Pacific to Europe rose 18% in the week of 17-23 August compared with late June, despite a steep fall in Chinese ecommerce traffic.
stories.whatHappened:
Freighter capacity from Asia Pacific to Europe has increased sharply since the EU introduced its new low-value import rules on 1 July. Rotate data show dedicated freighter capacity from Asia Pacific to Europe 18% higher in the week of 17-23 August than 22-28 June, the final full week before the new rules took effect. That compares with an increase of just 2% in the prior period, according to The Loadstar.

The increase in freighter capacity has occurred despite a steep fall in Chinese ecommerce traffic into Europe following the EU's elimination of the low-value import exemption. The new rules require customs declarations and VAT payment on all imports, regardless of value, which has reduced the volume of small parcels shipped by air from China to Europe.
stories.whyItMatters:
Air freighter capacity is rising while ecommerce volumes are falling, which means carriers are betting on non-ecommerce cargo to fill the planes. That cargo is your stock. If you ship air freight to Europe, you have more capacity available now than you did in June, which should push rates down. But rates have not moved yet, which means carriers are either holding the line or demand from other sectors is absorbing the freed-up capacity.

The EU's low-value import rule change has killed the ecommerce air freight model for small parcels, but it has not killed demand for air freight. Carriers are redeploying that capacity to higher-value cargo, which includes your stock if you ship samples, tooling, or fast-moving SKUs by air. You have pricing power right now if you are willing to negotiate.

If you were using an ecommerce platform that relied on the low-value exemption to ship air freight to Europe, that model is dead. You either absorb the VAT and customs cost, or you switch to sea freight and add lead time. The capacity freed up by ecommerce parcels means you have more air freight options if you need them, but you need to negotiate the rate.
stories.hotTake: Carriers added 18% more freighter capacity in six weeks, which means they saw this coming and positioned for it. They are not dumb. They will fill those planes with non-ecommerce cargo, and if you are shipping air freight to Europe, you should be demanding a better rate because the capacity is there.
actions: Renegotiate your Asia-Europe air freight rates if you have not already, because capacity is up 18%
Switch from ecommerce air parcel services to traditional air freight if you ship samples or fast-moving SKUs to Europe
Model the VAT and customs cost for any remaining low-value shipments and decide whether air freight still makes sense

faq.question: How long are ships waiting to berth at Shanghai and Ningbo right now?
faq.answer: Ships are waiting 10 days to berth at Shanghai and Ningbo as of 1 September 2026. Typhoon Saudel hit last week and added to congestion from earlier typhoons. The ports resumed operations on Friday, but vessel bunching and backlogs mean the queue will take weeks to clear. Linerlytica estimates 3.92 million TEU are waiting worldwide, 11% of the global fleet. Add two weeks to your transit assumptions.

faq.question: Will ocean freight rates drop in 2027 if carriers return to Suez?
faq.answer: Rates will drop if carriers return to Suez, but timing depends on how fast it happens. Sea-Intelligence modelled three scenarios. If only 19% of Asia-Europe services use Suez, global head-haul demand growth slows to 3.8% in H1 2027. If all services return, demand contracts 8.7%. Suez routing cuts 10 days off the round trip, freeing capacity and pushing rates down. Model a 15% reduction starting Q1 2027.

faq.question: Why is air freighter capacity to Europe increasing if ecommerce volumes are falling?
faq.answer: Carriers are redeploying capacity from ecommerce parcels to higher-value cargo. The EU eliminated the low-value import exemption on 1 July, killing the air freight model for small parcels. Freighter capacity from Asia Pacific to Europe rose 18% in the week of 17-23 August compared with late June. Carriers are filling planes with non-ecommerce cargo including samples and fast-moving SKUs. Renegotiate if you ship air freight to Europe.

faq.question: How will Cosco's new ship orders affect freight rates?
faq.answer: Cosco's 18 new ships will add 1.89 million TEU between 2028 and 2030, pushing rates down unless demand absorbs it. The global orderbook hit a record 14.84 million TEU, 43.1% of the current fleet. Deliveries are concentrated in 2028 to 2030, so you have two years of tight capacity followed by a flood of new tonnage. Lock in 2027 rates now and renegotiate in 2028 when newbuilds arrive.

faq.question: Should I book Q4 peak season shipments now or wait for rates to drop?
faq.answer: Book now. Vessel availability is tight because 11% of the global fleet is in berthing queues. Carriers have less capacity to sell, and charter rates are high as newbuilding deliveries fell to a three-year low in August. You either book early and pay the rate, or book late and pay more. The typhoon season is not over. If you are planning a November shipment and have not booked, you are already behind.
